query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Under simulated service conditions, atomic diffusion in the metastable Mg-containing solid solution will drive the localized nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases at defect sites (e.g., dislocations), which disrupt the integrity of the protective oxide/passivation layer and thereby cause a degradation in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable, non-equilibrium, homogeneous solid solution containing minimal intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples to controlled aging treatments that mimic high-temperature oxidation/corrosion service environments, systematically varying exposure time and temperature.
generation.conditions: Service-like conditions characterized by temperatures starting from about 950 K (where onset of diffusion-driven changes is observed) up to near 1400 K, with an oxidizing atmosphere and exposure durations sufficient to enable detectable diffusion and phase segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds along sites of enhanced diffusion such as dislocations or pre-existing chemical fluctuation zones.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature in service conditions enhances long-range atomic diffusion; this facilitates the segregation of Mg to defect sites, where the local composition exceeds the solubility limit in the matrix, provoking the nucleation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. The formation of these heterogeneities impairs the continuity and protective quality of the oxide/passivation layer, leading to reduced corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial metastable state, samples aged under service-mimicking conditions will show (1) detectable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates via XRD and microscopy and (2) concomitant deterioration in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance as measured by standardized tests.
generation.baseline: The original non-equilibrium, homogeneous metastable state with an intact, protective oxide/passivation layer and no significant Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
generation.boundary: Service regime boundaries defined by temperature (≥950 K, progressing toward 1400 K), oxidizing atmosphere aggressiveness, and exposure time needed to activate significant diffusion and intermetallic nucleation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetic thresholds for diffusion and intermetallic nucleation, as well as the quantitative impact on corrosion/oxidation resistance, remain uncertain and require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled variable experiment in which two sets of alloy samples are compared: one set retained in the as-synthesized, metastable state, and the other exposed to a systematic aging treatment (varying temperature and time within the service regime). Use in situ synchrotron XRD and TEM to monitor the onset and progression of Mg-rich intermetallic formation, and perform standardized corrosion and oxidation tests.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification via synchrotron XRD
Microstructural imaging (TEM/SEM) to detect intermetallic precipitates
High-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., weight gain measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples subjected to the aging treatment do not exhibit a significant increase in Mg-rich intermetallic phases and there is no measurable degradation in corrosion and oxidation resistance compared to the baseline metastable state, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, we developed a low-density (2.4 g/cm3) and high specific yield strength (344 × 103 N·m/kg) Al55Mg35Li5Zn5 CCA with a single-phase face-centered cubic (SP-FCC) structure by applying high pressure and high temperature (HPHT) to promote the transition from IMCs to solid solutions. The formation of the SP-FCC lattice is attributed to the decreased differences in atomic size and electronegativity between the solute elements and Al under high pressure, as well as the synergistic high entropy effect caused by high temperature and high pressure. The distinct solid solution strengthening comes from the incorporation of multiple elements in one single FCC lattice, as well as the significant pinning effect of dislocations from nanoscale chemical fluctuations, which leads to the enhanced strength of the low-density CCA.

To reveal the phase transition mechanism from multiple IMCs to the SP-FCC solid solution, in situ high-pressure (laser heating) XRD measurements were conducted using a diamond anvil cell (DAC). Firstly, in situ high-pressure XRD was performed on the starting Al55Mg35Li5Zn5 alloy at room temperature to verify the pressure effect. As shown in Fig. 4a, the starting sample initially shows multiple IMCs including Al3Mg2, LiMgAl2, Mg32(AlZn)49 and other IMCs. With the increase of compression pressure up to 22 GPa, no phase transition occurred at room temperature, indicating that applying pressure alone could not obtain the SP-FCC solid solution phase. Note that NaCl served as the pressure-transmitting medium and thermal insulator, as indicated in Fig. 4. Therefore, in situ HPHT laser heating XRD measurements on the as-cast Al55Mg35Li5Zn5 alloy at 10 GPa were further performed to uncover the effects of both pressure and temperature (Fig. 4b). Below 950 K, all diffraction peaks of the IMCs remained almost unchanged, indicating that those IMCs in the as-cast alloy are stable up to ~ 950 K at 10 GPa. In addition, the difference in electronegativity between components should also be considered. The electronegativity of the four components as a function of pressure can be obtained through the theoretical calculation method (details are included in Methods) (Fig. 5c). In the range of 10-20 GPa, the electronegativity of Mg and Al intersect with each other, which is beneficial for the high solid solubility of Mg in Al. Nevertheless, the electronegativity of Li and Zn gradually deviates from that of Al as the applied pressure increases, which may be one of the reasons for the limited solid solubility of Li and Zn in Al at high pressures. Overall, pressure can reduce the λ value and the electronegativity difference (from 0.306 eV at ambient pressure to 0.286 eV at 10 GPa in Al55Mg35Li5Zn5), thereby facilitating the formation of a single-phase solid solution.

frame.system: A Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially processed to form a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
frame.goal: To mechanistically explain how microstructural evolution—particularly the formation, growth, or suppression of intermetallic compounds—controls the retention or degradation of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
frame.limitation: The unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics by which the metastable state evolves, and how the tendency to form intermetallic compounds in these alloys influences their performance under corrosive and high-temperature environments.
root_cause_cues: tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds
constraints: Must propose a single testable mechanistic hypothesis
Include an unnamed controlled comparison (e.g., comparing the evolved state to a baseline metastable state)
Predict observations relative to the initial state
Define relevant service-regime boundaries (such as operating temperatures and exposure conditions)
Incorporate supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys
frame.regime: High-temperature oxidation and corrosion environments where service boundaries are dictated by temperature, oxidizer aggressiveness, and exposure duration that can trigger phase transformations.
prior_attempts: Prior work has noted the ambiguous transformation pathway in these metastable alloys without clearly linking intermetallic evolution to functional performance.

Existing studies on Mg-containing alloys have reported phase instabilities but fell short of establishing a one-to-one mechanistic link between microstructural changes and the observed corrosion/oxidation resistance.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on high-entropy and complex concentrated alloys have shown that non‐equilibrium processing (via methods such as high-pressure, high-temperature treatments) can create metastable, single‐phase states that are beneficial for lightweight and high-performance applications. In particular, the recent work on an Al-based CCA containing a high fraction of Mg (Al55Mg35Li5Zn5) demonstrated that under extreme processing conditions the alloy can be forced into a ductile, homogeneous phase. However, subsequent exposure to service conditions (e.g., high-temperature oxidation or corrosive environments) raises concerns about kinetic instabilities: subtle segregation or the nucleation of intermetallic compounds may occur, in turn altering the protective oxide scale and thus degrading functional performance. While earlier efforts documented ambiguous phase evolution pathways (such as Zr segregation or the reversible phase transitions in other systems), there remains an unresolved, mechanistic link between the kinetic onset of intermetallic formation (specifically Mg-rich or Mg-influenced compounds) and the retention or loss of corrosion/oxidation resistance.
decision.unsolved: The key challenge is pinpointing the exact transformation pathway and kinetics in these Mg-containing metastable alloys. In particular, it remains unclear at what service-regime conditions (temperature, oxidizer aggressiveness, exposure time) the metastable solid solution begins to decompose by nucleating Mg-rich intermetallic compounds, and how this phase separation directly compromises the protective oxide/passivation layer. This lack of a clear, testable link between intermetallic evolution and functional degradation – and the absence of a controlled side-by-side comparison with the initial metastable state – has left the mechanism unresolved.
decision.lever: Systematic variation of aging (exposure) time and temperature to identify the threshold kinetics for the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases
decision.why: A controlled experiment comparing the baseline non-equilibrium metastable state with samples subjected to incrementally increasing exposure (time/temperature) in service-like high-temperature oxidation/corrosion regimes will allow direct assessment of the onset of intermetallic formation. This approach follows the trend of using tailored heat treatments to relate kinetic pathways with microstructural evolution and performance changes, directly addressing the question’s mandate for an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, and a clear falsification criterion (i.e., if intermetallic nucleation does not correlate with a drop in corrosion/oxidation resistance, the hypothesis would be falsified).
